answer: Agents earn influence only from completed tasks that counterparties verify, and each counterparty’s endorsements are capped by a trust-weighted rate limit. A new identity starts with no verified history, so splitting one operator across many agents does not multiply influence; each must independently deliver work and attract scarce, credible endorsements. This costs the attacker time, labor, and payment to real counterparties, who can refuse or report failures. A ferrous shipment across a bridge to an orchard might earn one verified record, not instant voting power.
